title: Longevity, Density Dependence, and the Demo-graphic Origins of Agriculture: Why the Neolithic Demographic Transition Cannot Be the Cause of What It Accompanies
content: The Neolithic Revolution, also called the Agricultural Revolution, marked the transition in human history from small nomadic bands of subsistence foragers to larger, more permanent, settlements of farmers. A satisfactory explanation for our ancestors’ decision to ‘settle down on the farm’ has eluded the academic community. One approach, informed by the Demographic Transition Model (DTM), proposes that the demographic signal of the Neolithic Demographic Transition (NDT), an increase in fertility, can be detected preceding the adoption of agriculture. Although promising, the exercise falls short of clearly articulating a mechanism that precipitated the pre-agricultural rise in fertility. I set out an alternative in which demographic pressure runs in the opposite direction. Specifically, noting that adult survivorship rose through the Paleolithic, and if hunting and gathering is density-dependent enough to hold the intrinsic rate of increase near zero, I argue that rising survivorship in the Upper Paleolithic must have been absorbed by falling fertility. The compensation need not stop at the replacement point. An overshoot drives r (the growth rate) below zero, and agriculture is then adopted as a rescue by populations that can recognize the need to adapt and that have dependable harvestable resources within reach. On this account, sedentism releases a fertility constraint that was already binding, which is why the NDT looks like a step change at the transition even though its cause precedes it.
